body_en:
## CBA analysis: why the 49ers hold all the cards in the Brandon Aiyuk case

Brandon Aiyuk is taking his social media drama to the extreme, but behind the noise lies a highly complex contractual power struggle in which the San Francisco 49ers front office clearly has the upper hand thanks to the Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA). An in-depth look at the levers, lists and millions at stake in this poker game.

## The context: noise on social media, silence on the field

On the football side, things have gone strikingly quiet around Brandon Aiyuk: since his severe knee injury (torn ACL and MCL) in the 2024 season, there have been no training videos or rehab updates at all in recent months. On social media, however, the wide receiver is making all the more noise. With provocative posts, videos criticizing the franchise, pointedly wearing a Washington Commanders cap and cryptic messages, he is evidently trying to force his release (a "cut"). His obvious goal: a fresh start alongside his college friend, Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels.

What looks on the surface like the usual social media drama of a disgruntled NFL star turns out, on closer inspection, to be a highly complex contractual standoff in which the front office under general manager John Lynch holds every strategic trump card thanks to the current CBA.

## 1. The foundation: what "guaranteed salary" really means

To understand the 49ers' leverage, you first have to grasp something that is often wrongly taken for granted in the NFL world: guaranteed salary. Unlike leagues such as the NBA or MLB, NFL contracts are not fully guaranteed by default. When the media talk about guaranteed amounts, what they essentially mean is contractual risk protection. It determines under which conditions the franchise is obliged to pay the agreed salary (the so-called Paragraph 5 base salary, or "P5 salary" for short) even if it wants to release the player.

Many guarantees start out as pure injury guarantees: the player is financially protected if he gets hurt during official team activities. But if the player is healthy and the franchise wants to release him for football reasons, this protection does not apply.

The crucial point: this protection works both ways. If a player refuses rehab, skips mandatory meetings or does not cooperate with the team doctors, that is a culpable breach of contract. Under the current CBA, this entitles the franchise to void even existing guarantees entirely.

That is exactly the lever the 49ers pulled: because Aiyuk boycotted his rehab after the ACL tear and stayed away from the team for months, all of his remaining guarantees for 2026 were officially voided in the fall of 2025 and he was placed on the Reserve/Left Team list. His salary is therefore completely unguaranteed, and San Francisco could release him without a single cent of new dead cap.

The fact that Aiyuk has so far not challenged this drastic step in court or through the NFLPA suggests that the franchise's evidence of his misconduct was contractually beyond doubt. These developments also fuel rumors that Aiyuk's knee may already have suffered lasting, chronic damage from the incomplete rehabilitation.

## 2. The arsenal of roster lists: six options, one decision

If Aiyuk reports to the 49ers at the start of training camp, he has to undergo the mandatory physical by the team doctors. Since he apparently has not completed any professionally supervised rehab for months, passing that physical is all but impossible. Which list San Francisco then chooses is a decision worth millions.

| Option | List | Salary | Counts against roster? | Clawback possible? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | PUP (Physically Unable to Perform) | ✅ Full | No (regular season) | No |
| B | NFI (Non-Football Injury) | ❌ No salary | No | Possible |
| C | DNR (Did Not Report) | ❌ No salary + $50,000/day fine | No | Possible |
| D | Reserve/Left Squad | ❌ No salary + suspension | No | Possible |
| E | Reserve/Retired | ❌ No salary | No | Possible |
| F | Commissioner Exempt List | ⛔ Not applicable: league authority only, not a team tool | | |

### Option A: PUP list

The PUP list applies to injuries sustained in official football activities. If Aiyuk lands here, San Francisco has to keep paying him in full, even though he neglected his rehab. During the regular season he does not take up one of the 53 roster spots, but he has to sit out at least four games. From the 49ers' point of view, this is the least attractive option.

### Option B: NFI list

The NFI list applies to injuries that happen away from the field. This is an important gray area: the 49ers can argue that Aiyuk's current inability to play is no longer the direct result of the 2024 injury but the result of grossly negligent neglect of his rehab. In that case the team is entitled to stop paying his salary entirely, meaning not a cent of the weekly P5 salary is paid out.

### Option C: DNR list, costs Aiyuk $50,000 a day

If Aiyuk stays away from camp without an excuse, the current CBA (since 2020) adds expensive fines: $50,000 per day, which the franchise is not legally allowed to waive. No salary, no roster spot, but damages on his side that grow every day.

### Option D: Reserve/Left Squad, the 49ers' real weapon

For players who abandon the team during the season. The 49ers already used this instrument against Aiyuk in December 2025. Placement on this list gives the franchise the ultimate proof of a forfeitable breach under CBA Article 4, Section 9, and opens the door to a massive clawback process, i.e. reclaiming signing bonus installments that have already been paid out (one fifth per year).

### Option E: Reserve/Retired, no escape through a fake retirement

If Aiyuk announces his retirement, the 49ers keep the exclusive rights to him. His contract is frozen. If he later wants to un-retire, he has to play out the remaining contract year with San Francisco on the old terms. A move to the Commanders is ruled out this way.

### Option F: Commissioner Exempt List, a misconception that does not apply

Only Commissioner Roger Goodell personally can place players on this list, and only for serious violations of the Personal Conduct Policy (e.g. domestic violence). It is therefore fundamentally not a tool for contract holdouts.

## 3. The critical date: what happens to $25 million on September 1

On September 1, 2026, the contract calls for a massive option bonus of just under $25 million. An option bonus is a popular salary cap tool: the team pays out a large sum in cash right away but may spread it over the remaining years of the contract for cap purposes, keeping the immediate cap hit low.

### What happens if the 49ers let the option lapse on September 1?

No automatic release. The unexercised option turns into a huge, unguaranteed base salary for the current season. Because Aiyuk is on a suspended reserve list, the 49ers do not have to pay that salary either. They save the full $25 million in cash and still keep the exclusive rights to him. So the supposed September 1 deadline is not really a deadline at all: just like with Trent Williams in March, it is simply a voluntary option for the team to save salary cap space.

### Tolling: the frozen contract

Because he plays no games, his contract is legally frozen at the end of the season (tolling). In spring 2027 he will face the same mess: a year older, not a cent earned, no game action, and still contractually bound to San Francisco.

### Clawback: reclaiming money already paid

Under CBA Article 4, Section 9 (Forfeiture of Salary), the 49ers can even reclaim money already paid because of the ongoing breach of contract. This concerns the 2024 signing bonus ($23 million in total, prorated at $4.6 million per year). By placing him on the Left Squad list in the winter of 2025, San Francisco has already laid the groundwork for an arbitration case and can demand back up to 100% of this year's installment ($4.6 million).

| Mechanism | Amount / consequence for Aiyuk | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Option bonus (not exercised) | Loses ≈ $25 million cash payment | Contract clause, Sept. 2026 |
| Loss of Paragraph 5 salary | No weekly salary | NFI / DNR / Left Squad list |
| DNR fine | $50,000 per day (cannot be waived) | CBA since 2020 |
| Clawback of 2026 signing bonus | Up to $4.6 million reclaimed | CBA Art. 4, Sec. 9 |
| Loss of accrued season | No progress toward free agency | CBA minimum participation rule |
| Tolling of the contract | Still bound to SF in 2027 | Standard CBA mechanism |

## 4. What options does Brandon Aiyuk have left?

By boycotting his medical care and running a loud social media campaign, the wide receiver has maneuvered himself into a dead end. His remaining strategic options are minimal:

- **Ask to be reinstated and pass the physical (report fit):** Aiyuk's only real way out. Because he is still on the Left Squad list, he first has to file a formal petition for reinstatement with the team and the league. Only once both have cleared him can Aiyuk enter the facility again. If the 49ers don't feel like dealing with the commotion, they can also suspend Aiyuk for up to four more weeks because of his conduct and request a roster exemption before he is allowed back. Only then comes the question of whether Aiyuk is even fit enough to pass a physical. And only once he is declared fully fit do the 49ers have to decide whether to cut him or attempt a fresh start.
- **Signal unconditional cooperation:** If the knee is not medically ready yet, he has to cooperate fully with the medical staff and prove that the delay is biological in nature. Only then can he avoid the NFI list and get onto the financially protected PUP list, after being cleared again by the league and the team.
- **Enable a trade by giving up salary:** No team will trade for an injured player in the middle of a legal dispute. Aiyuk and his agent would have to signal to potential trade partners that he is fit and willing to restructure his unguaranteed contract drastically right after a trade.
- **Provoking a release, a strategy with hard limits:** Aiyuk's current strategy is running into financial and administrative limits. Since he costs the team neither money nor a roster spot while on the reserve lists, San Francisco has no reason whatsoever to give in to this pressure.

## Conclusion: the 49ers can simply sit this out

For the San Francisco 49ers front office there is basically no reason to act hastily. San Francisco can let September 1 pass without doing anything, park Aiyuk on one of the suspended roster lists without any financial obligation or cap charge, and at the same time send a signal to the entire league.

The franchise's broader interest: this strict course is likely to be very much in line with the wishes of the other NFL owners. A dangerous precedent must be avoided, namely that a player can force his way out of an existing contract through a rehab strike, provocative behavior and social media campaigns without any financial consequences.

The burden is therefore entirely on the player. Brandon Aiyuk has to prove that he is both physically fully ready to play again and willing to cooperate professionally and return to the league. After months away from the field and no sign whatsoever of a full recovery, there are big question marks behind both. If he cannot provide that proof, instead of the move to Washington he is hoping for, he faces permanent football exile and, in the worst case, a premature end to his career.
